issues.legal_issue: A grant of taxation powers by reference to municipal powers includes later amendments to the municipal laws when the laws operate together and the authority has no independent taxation machinery.
material_facts: The development authority was given taxation powers by reference to the powers of municipal bodies under two municipal laws.
The development authority’s governing law provided no independent taxation power or machinery and relied on those municipal laws.
The property-tax provisions were added to the municipal laws after the development authority received its taxation powers.
issues.conclusion: The authority could exercise the municipal taxation powers in force when it sought to tax, including those created by later amendments.
issues.legal_principle: Incorporation of specific provisions of an earlier enactment ordinarily does not import later amendments to that enactment. A mere reference to powers under another enactment, particularly where the enactments are supplemental and the referring enactment has no independent machinery, is read as referring to the powers in force when they are exercised. The Court relied on Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindustan Co-operative Insurance Society, Ltd., Clarke v. Bradlaugh, Collector of Customs, Madras v. Nathella Samathu Chetty, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan.

rule.if: tax_demand_appeal and authority_power_referenced and no_independent_tax_machinery and later_municipal_amendment

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.authority_power_referenced: The authority received taxation powers by reference to the powers of municipal bodies under other laws.
predicates.no_independent_tax_machinery: The authority’s governing law provided no independent taxation power or machinery.
predicates.later_municipal_amendment: The municipal laws were amended after the authority received its taxation powers.

issues.definition: When a property-tax appeal concerns an authority whose powers are referred to rather than independently provided, and the governing laws operate together, the municipal powers in force when exercised apply despite later amendments.

issues.legal_issue: A property tax imposed directly by its governing provisions does not require compliance with procedures prescribed for imposing other municipal taxes.
material_facts: The property-tax provisions directly stated that property tax was to be charged, levied and paid on lands or buildings.
The authority demanded property tax under those provisions.
The company argued that the procedures prescribed for other taxes had not been followed.
issues.conclusion: The authority was not required to follow the procedures prescribed for imposing other municipal taxes before levying the property tax.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 127A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 and 135 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 directly create the property-tax liability and right to levy it. The procedures in sections 129 and 133 respectively concern taxes imposed under sections 127 and 132, not property tax imposed under sections 127A and 135. Section 133(4) further confirms that the procedure in section 133 does not apply to the property tax charged under section 135.

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.direct_property_tax_charge: The governing property-tax provision itself directs that the tax be charged, levied and paid.
predicates.procedure_limited_to_other_taxes: The cited procedural requirements govern the imposition of other taxes rather than the property tax.

issues.definition: When a property-tax demand is made under a direct property-tax charge and the cited procedure applies to other taxes, that procedure is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A taxing authority has no discretion to choose whether to tax land, buildings, or both when the property-tax provision makes the applicable charge depend on the property present.
material_facts: The property-tax provisions addressed lands, buildings, or both.
The company argued that the taxing authority had to decide whether it wished to tax the land, the buildings, or both.
issues.conclusion: The authority had to impose the tax on the land, the buildings, or both as applicable; the provisions gave it no choice among them.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 127A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 and 135 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 require tax on land where land alone is taxable, on buildings where buildings alone are taxable, and on both where both are taxable. The Court treated this as the plain meaning of the provisions.

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.property_tax_charge_covers_land_and_buil: The governing property-tax charge covers land, buildings, or both, depending on the property present.
predicates.taxable_property_present: The property includes land, buildings, or both that fall within the charge.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a charge covering land and buildings and taxable property is present, the tax applies to each category of property covered by the charge.

issues.legal_issue: Property owned by a separately incorporated company is not exempt from property tax merely because the government owns all of the company’s shares.
material_facts: The companies were incorporated under the Companies Act and owned the lands and buildings at issue.
The government had subscribed the companies’ entire share capital.
The companies claimed exemption on the ground that their property was government property.
issues.conclusion: The companies’ property was not exempt as property of the Union merely because the government owned all their shares.
issues.legal_principle: Article 285(1) of the Constitution and the exemptions in section 127A(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 and section 136 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 concern property of the Union, not property owned by a separate corporate person whose shares the Union owns. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar, Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Income-tax Officer, and Tamlin v. Hansaford.

rule.if: tax_demand_appeal and company_owns_taxed_property and government_owns_all_shares and company_has_separate_legal_personality

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.company_owns_taxed_property: The taxed land or buildings are owned by a company.
predicates.government_owns_all_shares: The government owns the company’s entire share capital.
predicates.company_has_separate_legal_personality: The company is incorporated as a legal person distinct from its shareholders.

issues.definition: When a company that is legally distinct from its government shareholder owns the taxed property, government ownership of all its shares does not make that property government property.

issues.legal_issue: The State’s power to tax land and buildings for municipal administration is not displaced merely because the property is used for mining subject to central regulation and development.
material_facts: The taxed lands and buildings were used for, or covered by, coal mines.
The tax was imposed as a tax on land and buildings by an authority performing municipal functions.
The challenge asserted that the tax conflicted with central powers over coal-mine regulation and development.
No evidence was presented that the tax impeded the achievement of the objectives of the central mining legislation.
issues.conclusion: The State’s power to confer the property-tax power on the authority did not conflict with the Union’s power to regulate and develop coal mines, and the tax did not defeat the purpose of the central legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The State Legislature’s powers over local government under Entry 5 and taxes on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II remain distinct from the Union’s powers over mine regulation and development under Entry 54 of List I. The declaration in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 does not occupy the field of municipal administration or invalidate a legitimate tax on land. The Court relied on H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor, State of Haryana v. Chanan Mal, and Ishwari Khetan Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and distinguished Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar. It also considered the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973.

rule.if: mining_tax_challenge and local_land_building_tax and tax_supports_municipal_functions and no_shown_mining_impediment

predicates.mining_tax_challenge: The proceeding challenges a local tax on the ground that it conflicts with central regulation of mining.
predicates.local_land_building_tax: The challenged levy is a tax on land or buildings.
predicates.tax_supports_municipal_functions: The authority imposing the tax performs municipal functions.
predicates.no_shown_mining_impediment: The record does not show that the tax impedes the objectives of central mining regulation or development.

issues.definition: When a challenged levy taxes land or buildings to support municipal functions and no mining-related impediment is shown, central mining regulation alone does not displace the State’s municipal taxing power.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement by an official to surrender a public authority’s taxation power beyond the scope authorized by the authority does not invalidate a later property-tax demand.
material_facts: The authority and the company entered an agreement under which the authority purported to refrain from imposing taxes and other charges in return for annual contributions.
The authority’s earlier decision had authorized giving up its right to impose octroi tax only.
The chairman entered the broader agreement, and the company relied on it to resist the property-tax demand.
issues.conclusion: The agreement did not bar the property-tax demand because the chairman acted beyond the authority conferred on him.
issues.legal_principle: The Court endorsed the High Court’s reasons for rejecting the waiver argument, particularly that the authority had decided to relinquish only its right to impose octroi tax and its chairman lacked authority to bind it to a broader surrender of taxation powers.

rule.if: tax_demand_appeal and claimed_tax_waiver and competent_body_authorized_only_limited_waiver and official_promised_broader_tax_immunity

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.claimed_tax_waiver: The taxpayer relies on an agreement said to waive the authority’s power to impose tax.
predicates.competent_body_authorized_only_limited_w: The authority’s competent body authorized waiver only of a limited category of tax.
predicates.official_promised_broader_tax_immunity: An official purported to promise immunity from a broader range of taxes than the competent body authorized.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer relies on a broad tax waiver but the authority authorized only a limited waiver, the broader promise by an official does not bar the tax demand.
